why: It gives a permanent roofed playhouse standing in a shrine town, the case nearest to the provincial-town theater this page draws. The article does not say the house stood on the shrine's own ground. It gives the building's measures as built, the one Edo-period playhouse whose size this record has read, but it cites no source for them (it lists the 1976 restoration report, which this record has not read). The house standing now was taken down, moved from its first site nearer the approach road and rebuilt in 1972-76, then reworked in 2003-04, so the article's seat count and floor area are for the rebuilt building. It says the town, as Kotohira's vermilion-seal and shogunal land, was loosely policed, which is why shows were allowed there. It was modeled on the Ōnishi theater, one of Osaka's three Dōtonbori houses (by another account on Osaka's Chikugo-za), which is the ground for taking its size for a city house, and a pilgrimage town's playhouse may have been smaller or larger than a capital's.

It dates the arrival in Japan of the London-type public watering trough, a Meiji import with no Edo-period counterpart in that form, and a newspaper headline it cites (Yomiuri, 1906-11-29) calls the 1906 one the first. It is of Japan only; it says nothing of China or Korea. That no earlier trough is named is the article's silence, not a finding that none existed. It does not describe how horses were watered before 1906, though its own lead photograph (a hollowed-log trough in Manchukuo) and its see-also line (Batō Kannon shrines stand by horse watering places throughout Japan) show that plainer watering places existed, undated. It carries the date of the London-type trough, not an absence of animal watering places in the premodern setting.

It shows a pavilion roof over every well of the Ming and Qing palace, and an iron pulley hung from beams over one of them. It says that in the Ming and Qing some well pavilions had pulleys, but it dates no single pavilion, and many palace buildings were rebuilt under the Qing. It calls the pulley "very likely" Qing from the Imperial Household Department's workshop archives, which record iron pulleys being made, not from the building itself. Nothing in it dates the roof or the pulley to the Ming in particular. It describes a palace, the richest possible case, so it says nothing of how often an ordinary town or village well had a roof.
It gives the size band of a hatamoto's residence, against which this page classes a compound.<!-- a scholarly paper on the granted residences would state it better -->.

It places the posting of edicts, the county magistrate's own notices and bans, verdicts and tax-arrears lists on the office's gate walls. Its Ming support is thin: it quotes the monthly edicts of 1519 from Shen Bang's Wanshu zaji, which the Ming emperor gave out orally and the people received at the county gate, but that they hung on the splayed walls is the author's own framing, and his passage on verdicts and tax-arrears lists speaks of county offices of old without a date. His one dated official posting at a county office's gate is Song (the Green Sprouts law, "posted at the county gate"). His one dated Qing example is Shanghai in 1853, a notice on the county office's wall that he does not tie to the gate walls. It speaks of Chinese offices generally, not of any one county, and of walls rather than a freestanding board; the later use of the screen wall facing the gate is undated, and its Kangxi-era notice of 1686 illustrates how notices were signed, not where that one was posted.

Its dated evidence is the inscription it reports on the Minle dou, carved in the fourth year of the Guangxu era (1878, late Qing), and its sketch of the polder's history: that its dikes, creeks and sluices made one irrigation system by the end of the eighteenth century, and a line it quotes from the polder's gazetteer, the Sangyuanwei zhi, under the year 1794 (the piece does not date the gazetteer itself), that in drought the people within the polder already had water for their fields. That history is the reporters' own, sourced only by that quotation. How the sluices work it gives in the present tense, in the words of today's city water bureau director, and for some sluices only: those hung with mitre ('人'-shaped) wooden gates open of themselves to drain the polder when the water within stands high, and close against the tide or flood without. It does not say the Minle dou is one of these, though it shows the dou's two heavy wooden gates; that the dou sits in the dike is implied, from its 'within' and 'without' the polder, rather than stated; and it says nothing of a sluice for each fish pond.

It defines the form our single-rampart capital follows and gives its largest example. The form is a late-Sengoku and Momoyama answer to a besieging army, systematized after the siege of Odawara, not an Edo-period peacetime norm - which bears on whether a capital of ours draws one rampart around its whole population.

It calls it a novel of the Ming dynasty, set in the Northern Song, and names a printed revision of the reign of Emperor Shizong (1522-1566) as the ancestor of the most widely read versions. It leaves the date of the first writing open between the late Yuan and the mid-Ming, so it dates the novel only to the Ming.
It states that artisans were a registered hereditary class bound to the government's works, which is the organization this page's kiln quarter rests on. It names no kilns or potters.

It quotes, in the original, the passage of the Koeki Kokusanko, a farm book of the late Edo period, on kunugi branching from about one jo up and cut in winter for Ikeda charcoal, which is premodern evidence for a cut-over oak wood of many thin stems. The seven-to-ten-year cycle it gives is present-day coppice practice for charcoal kunugi, and the book it quotes describes one charcoal district, not woods in general.
It dates the journey the diary records, which the Wikisource text of the chapter does not state.

It dates the edition whose scanned text this record's Huc citations quote, which the scanned text itself does not show. The 1855 is the date of this English edition by Harper, not of the account itself: the French original, L'Empire chinois, appeared in Paris in 1854. Huc's travels through China were in 1844-1846, so this date cannot date anything he describes. The scanner's own note on the page calls the exact publication date unknown; the 1855 is the catalog's.

It states that irrigation water was held and allocated by village associations under customary practice and that the order of intake was itself fought over in the courts, which is why this page will not give a kawata quarter a headwater tap. It is Japanese only. The article is a stub marked for expansion.

It states that intakes drawn since before 1896 hold customary right under the modern law, which is the durability of a village's water right this page rests on. It is about Japanese law and says nothing of China. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. The inference backward from a modern statute's recognition of old custom to the durability of a premodern village's right is this page's own.

unsettled: A reconstruction from an undated survey of an unplaced workshop, so the period of its evidence cannot be fixed by the table.
